title: Super-molasses returns: All optical near-resonance laser cooling and trapping of neutral atoms from background vapor
authors: Matt Himsworth, Chester Camm, Max Carey, Jack Saywell, Jonathan Woods, Vilius Atkoucius, Florence Concepcion, Konstantinos Karakostas, Hannah Brady, Doruk Tan Atila, Ellie Heywood, Alex Jantzen, Andrei Dragomir, Christopher Morley, James Bateman
abstract: Laser cooled and trapped atoms have been the workhorse of atomic physics for the past four decades. The predominant method has been the highly versatile Magneto-Optical Trap. We describe an alternative laser trap involving a simple geometry of collimated laser beams that provides both a velocity and position dependent restoring force such that a dense cloud of cold atoms is formed. This technique produces similar atom number ($>10^6$) and density ($10^{10}$\,atoms/cm$^{3}$) to the Magneto-Optical Trap, albeit with \emph{no magnetic field}. The beam geometry is compatible with conventional sub-Doppler cooling techniques, allowing the trapped cloud to be cooled to $< 10~μ$K. We demonstrate the validity and robustness of the trap by capturing $^{87}$Rb atoms directly from the background vapor and provide a theoretical discussion of the underlying principles. This trap has many unique properties that make it highly suitable for quantum sensing, timing, and computing applications as well as a new tool in fundamental science and metrology.
summary: The authors introduce the Super-Molasses Trap (SMT), a novel method to cool and trap dense clouds of neutral atoms using only intersecting laser beams, completely eliminating the need for external magnetic fields. The technique achieves performance comparable to MOTs—including high atom numbers and sub-$\mu	ext{K}$ temperatures—making it a powerful new tool for quantum applications.
main_problem: To describe an alternative laser cooling and trapping method for neutral atoms that operates without relying on a magnetic field, overcoming limitations associated with traditional Magneto-Optical Traps (MOTs).
main_result: The Super-Molasses Trap (SMT) successfully traps dense clouds of cold atoms ($>10^6$ atoms at $\sim 2 	imes 10^{10} 	ext{atoms/cm}^3$) using only laser beams, achieving sub-$\mu	ext{K}$ temperatures.
method: The technique utilizes a simple geometry of retro-reflected collimated laser beams in a tripod configuration to create a position and velocity dependent restoring force, supplemented by an 'optical molasses' stage for final cooling.
model_or_system: The system involves trapping neutral atoms (e.g., $^{87}	ext{Rb}$) from background vapor using intersecting, misaligned laser beams that form a dissipative optical lattice structure, contrasting with the magnetic field dependence of MOTs.
key_observables: Atom number ($>2 	imes 10^6$), density ($\sim 2 	imes 10^{10} 	ext{atoms/cm}^3$), ensemble temperature (cooled to sub-$\mu	ext{K}$), and trap loading rate ($2 	imes 10^7 	ext{atoms/s}$).
important_parameters: Laser detuning ($	ext{-}1\Gamma$ optimal), laser power ($22 	ext{mW/cm}^2$), background vapor pressure (optimal near $2 	imes 10^{-9} 	ext{mbar}$), and the absence of magnetic field dependence.
main_assumptions: The trapping mechanism is believed to utilize principles related to super-molasses cooling within a near-resonant dipole trap, although a full quantitative theoretical explanation remains elusive.
figures_summary: Figures show the laser beam geometry (tripod), the dependence of atom number on detuning/power, and temperature reduction curves demonstrating the effectiveness of the optical molasses stage.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the SMT as an alternative to MOTs, details the experimental setup and measurements (atom number, density, cooling), compares performance metrics, discusses stability and loading rates, and concludes with a theoretical discussion on the underlying physics.
why_interesting: This work presents a robust, field-free alternative to established trapping methods, which is highly relevant for quantum sensing and metrology where magnetic shielding or field gradients are undesirable. The investigation into the fundamental mechanism of super-molasses cooling touches upon complex non-equilibrium dynamics in open quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Left: The laser beam geometry used in this paper to produce the super-molasses trap, with incident (green) beams forming a tripod and angled from the vertical by 35◦and retro-reflected (red) beams misaligned by very small angles. Polarization is linear as shown in blue, although the trap can operate with circular and combinations of polarization. Right: A (inverted greyscale) fluorescence image of the trapped ensemble of rubidium atoms. The laser beams have been aligned to produce an extended cloud to highlight the lattice structure. The vertical dimension of the cloud is approximately 3 mm. Denser and more spherical clouds can be obtained with different beam reflection angles.

FIG. 2: A photograph of the SMT taken along the z-axis of Figure 1). The three retro-reflected beams can be seen scattering on the top chamber window, at the center of which is the brighter cold atom cloud.

FIG. 3: Dependence of atom number in the SMT on laser detuning and power. We see a peak of approximately 2.5 million atoms at -1 Γ detuning and 10 mW per beam. The peak atom number is highly dependent on beam alignments but once a global maximum is found the atom number is quite consistent for the same beam width.

FIG. 4: Top: The trapped ensemble temeratues before the ’molasses’ stage for a selection of detunings. The solid lines are linear fits to guide the eye, and the dashed line indicates the Doppler Temperature for 87Rb. Middle: The trapped ensemble temperature after a ‘molasses’ stage during which the laser detuning is shifted to the displayed frequency in 2 ms, whilst the power is linearly ramped down to different final values. Solid lines are linear fits to guide the eye. Bottom: An example of the ensemble radius expansion data (dots) used calculate the temperature (lines). We see the temperature is uniform along both axes.

FIG. 5: The Allan Deviation of the trap centre (Top) and size (Bottom) over several timescales. The center is determined by fitting of a 2D Gaussian to absorption image. Short term instability is dominated by vibrations of the undamped table due to nearby traffic.
